name: New Windsor / Novaya Windsorka
description:
New Windsor sits across the Detroit River from the GLMZ's industrial heartland, and that proximity defines everything about it. The Ambassador Bridge — reinforced, widened, and draped in sensor arrays — and the Detroit-Windsor Tunnel form the two arteries connecting Canadian sovereign territory to the American corporate zones, and every drop of commerce that flows between them gets taxed, scanned, and surveilled twice. Once by each side. The result is a city that exists primarily as a jurisdictional membrane — a place where goods, people, and data change legal status simply by crossing a river.

The old automotive plants that once built cars for the North American market have been retooled into fabrication centers for neural interface components, autonomous vehicle subsystems, and military-grade augmentation hardware. Tessera Corponation and Zheng-Dao Bioelectric both maintain sovereign manufacturing enclaves here, exploiting the dual-sovereignty arrangement to dodge regulations on both sides of the border. Workers commute between jurisdictions daily, their legal rights flickering on and off like a bad connection as they cross the river. Canadian labor protections apply on the north bank. Corporate sovereign law applies on the south. The tunnel between is a legal no-man's-land where neither applies and everyone knows it.

The residential districts sprawl south and east from the riverfront, a patchwork of climate-refugee housing blocks, mid-tier corporate dormitories, and the decaying bones of twentieth-century suburbia that nobody has bothered to demolish. The population skews young, transient, and bilingual in ways that have nothing to do with French and English — the Gray Zone Cant, Mandarin trade pidgin, and machine-interface shorthand are the languages that actually matter here. The city smells like ozone and river water, and on bad days the chemical plumes from Sarnia drift east and add a third note that makes your eyes water.

sights: The Ambassador Bridge lit with customs scanning arrays, a neon-traced spine over black water
Fabrication centers running 24-hour shifts, robotic arms visible through translucent walls
Dual-sovereignty markers on every street corner — Canadian maple leaf on one side, corporate logo on the other
The Detroit skyline across the river, arcology towers dwarfing everything on the Windsor side
Climate-refugee housing blocks with laundry strung between balconies, a defiant splash of color against grey concrete
sounds: The low thrum of tunnel traffic — a vibration you feel in your teeth more than hear
Customs drones overhead, their scanning pings a constant irritant
Fabrication equipment running triple shifts — the sound of money being made for someone else
River barges sounding horns in the pre-dawn fog
Arguments in three languages at once at the bridge checkpoints
smells: Ozone from the bridge scanning arrays
Detroit River water — industrial, metallic, and alive despite everything
Chemical drift from Sarnia on east winds, sharp enough to taste
Fabrication coolant from the manufacturing enclaves
atmosphere.feel: A city that exists in the hyphen between two systems. Everyone here is performing a jurisdictional magic trick — they are Canadian citizens and corporate subjects simultaneously, and the trick only works as long as nobody examines it too closely. The tension is mundane, quotidian, built into the commute.

demographics: Population 1.2 million registered, an estimated 300,000 undocumented transients cycling through. Heavy representation of climate refugees from the American Gulf Coast who crossed through Detroit and kept going. Dual-citizenship holders make up 40% of the workforce — people who carry two legal identities and trust neither.
economy: Manufacturing and border commerce. The fabrication enclaves produce augmentation components for export to GLMZ. The tunnel and bridge generate customs revenue that funds what passes for municipal government. Smuggling — of goods, data, and people — accounts for an estimated 25% of actual economic activity, and everyone from the customs agents to the corponations takes a cut.
power_structure: Nominally Canadian municipal government, practically a joint administration between the Canadian Border Authority and the corporate sovereigns who maintain manufacturing enclaves. Tessera and Zheng-Dao have more employees in Windsor than the city has civil servants. The mayor is elected; the mayor is irrelevant.
dangers: Dual-sovereignty jurisdiction traps — commit an act legal in Canada but illegal in corporate territory, and you can be arrested on the bridge
Chemical exposure from Sarnia drift events — the air quality warnings come after the damage is done
Corporate labor disputes that escalate into physical lockdowns of entire districts
Smuggling operations that treat human cargo the same as any other inventory
The tunnel's legal no-man's-land, where disappearances happen and no jurisdiction investigates
opportunities: Border arbitrage — legal in one jurisdiction, profitable in the other
Fabrication work for the skilled — augment technicians are always in demand
Intelligence brokerage — information about corporate activity in Windsor is valuable in Detroit and vice versa
Refugee networks that connect Windsor to every displaced community in the GLMZ
story_hooks: A fabrication worker discovers the augmentation components she's building contain an undocumented surveillance substrate — and the specs came from both sides of the border
The tunnel's ventilation system is being retrofitted with neural-frequency emitters — crowd control infrastructure disguised as air quality management
A dual-sovereignty legal case threatens to collapse the entire jurisdictional framework that Windsor's economy depends on

adjacent_to: Blackpipe Corridor (Sarnia, east along the chemical coast)

frequented_by: Border runners and smugglers working the tunnel
Corporate security personnel monitoring the enclaves
